jsonld.name: Retirement & Safe Withdrawal Rate (FIRE) Calculator
jsonld.description: Calculate your FIRE number from a safe withdrawal rate, when you'll reach financial independence, Coast FIRE, and how long an inflation-adjusted retirement portfolio lasts.

acceptedAnswer.text: A guideline from William Bengen's 1994 research: withdraw 4% of your portfolio in the first year of retirement, then increase that dollar amount with inflation each year. Historically this lasted at least 30 years for a balanced US stock and bond portfolio. It implies a savings target of about 25× your annual spending.

mainEntity.name: How much do I need to retire?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide your expected annual spending by your safe withdrawal rate: $60,000 a year at 4% needs $1.5 million, at 3.5% about $1.71 million. Subtract any Social Security or pension income from spending first.

Coast FIRE is the point where your existing investments, left to grow with no new contributions, will reach your full FIRE number by your target retirement age. After that you only need to earn enough to cover current expenses.
Yes. Retirement withdrawals rise with your inflation rate every year, the FIRE projection compares your portfolio to an inflation-adjusted target, and the chart shows balances in today's dollars.

mainEntity.name: What return rate should I assume?

acceptedAnswer.text: Long-run US stock returns have averaged roughly 10% a year before inflation, and a balanced portfolio less. Many planners use 6–8% while saving and 4–6% in retirement, when portfolios usually hold more bonds. Returns vary widely from year to year and are not guaranteed.

mainEntity.name: How does Social Security change how much I need saved?

acceptedAnswer.text: Social Security covers part of most retirees' expenses, so subtract your expected annual benefit from your target spending before applying the withdrawal rate — you likely need less saved than a benefit-blind calculation suggests.
